name: Château de Codignat

highlights: A 12th-century castle whose last lord, Charles Henri-Théoda d'Estaing, was guillotined in 1794
Owned between the wars by Prince Obolenski, a descendant of the last Russian Tsar
A Relais & Châteaux member for over 30 years, reopened as an intimate château d'hôtes after a 2021 closure
description:
Château de Codignat is a 12th-century castle in the Basse-Auvergne countryside. In 1754, Charles Antoine Claude de Chazerat, Intendant of the Generality of Riom, became owner. It later passed to the d'Estaing family — Charles-François d'Estaing served as Lieutenant General of the King's armies, while the last lord, Charles Henri-Théoda d'Estaing, was guillotined in 1794.

Its roof was restored in the Viollet-le-Duc style in the early 20th century. Between the wars, it was owned by Prince Obolenski, a descendant of the last Russian Tsar. The château became a hotel in 1971 and has been a Relais & Châteaux member for over 30 years. After changing hands several times — the Baglioni Group, then Sorgente Hotels & Resorts, which earned it a fifth star in 2012 — it closed in 2021 and was acquired by Groupe DIES, reopening as an intimate château d'hôtes. Today its 19 rooms and suites (14 rooms and 5 suites, two of them duplex) are split between the historic castle, the Chalet Myrtille (an independent building in the park with its own living room, patio, and two bedrooms across two floors), and a separate Cottage.

The execution of the château's last lord, Charles Henri-Théoda d'Estaing, during the French Revolution ties Codignat directly to the violent upheaval that swept away much of the pre-revolutionary French aristocracy.

Prince Obolenski's interwar ownership, as a descendant of the last Russian Tsar, connects this Auvergne castle to the broader diaspora of Russian nobility who settled across Western Europe following the 1917 revolution.

The château's repeated changes of corporate ownership — from Baglioni to Sorgente to Groupe DIES, with a 2021 closure in between — reflects the volatile hospitality-industry history that has affected even long-established Relais & Châteaux properties.

The surrounding volcanic Chaîne des Puys, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the city of Clermont-Ferrand give guests staying at Codignat access to one of central France's most distinctive natural landscapes.

faqs.question: Are all the rooms at Château de Codignat within the historic castle?
faqs.answer: No — most are, but the Chalet Myrtille (an independent building with its own living room and patio) and a separate Cottage in the park also offer guest accommodation.

faqs.question: What happened to Château de Codignat's last lord?
faqs.answer: Charles Henri-Théoda d'Estaing, the castle's last lord, was guillotined in 1794 during the French Revolution.

faqs.question: Why did Château de Codignat close in 2021?
faqs.answer: The property changed corporate ownership several times (Baglioni Group, then Sorgente Hotels & Resorts) before closing in 2021; it was subsequently acquired by Groupe DIES and reopened as a more intimate château d'hôtes.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** In Bort-l'Étang, Puy-de-Dôme, Basse-Auvergne — within reach of Clermont-Ferrand.

**Rooms & rates:** 19 rooms and suites from €155/night; most are within the 12th-century castle, with additional accommodation in the freestanding Chalet Myrtille and a separate Cottage in the park.

**On-site:** Park grounds with a dedicated events building, restaurant, and Viollet-le-Duc-restored roofline.

**Good to know:** A genuinely storied property — Russian imperial connections (Prince Obolenski between the wars) alongside a French Revolutionary-era history (its last lord was guillotined in 1794) — recently repositioned as a more intimate château d'hôtes after a 2021 closure and change of ownership.

**Combine with:** Clermont-Ferrand and the volcanic Chaîne des Puys (UNESCO), both within driving distance.
